technical.intro: You don't write code. You reason about how software works well enough to talk to engineers and spot risk. Conceptual is enough — except SQL and market sizing, which you should actually practice.

chain.note: Most of the technical skills are one story. A request travels this path; the rest are about making it fast, safe, and measurable.
labels: the app or browser the user taps
extras: Caching sits in front of the database so common answers don't get recomputed.
Latency is the total round trip. Slow here is a product problem.
A data pipeline copies the events out to a place you can query for metrics.

skills.name: APIs
skills.gist: How one service asks another for data.
need: An API is a contract — a fixed way to ask, and a fixed shape of answer.
Ask "is there already an API for this?" before assuming something must be built.
Every new API a feature depends on is a new thing that can break or slow down.
skills.assess: I can explain what an API is and why two teams agree on a contract before building against each other.

skills.name: Databases
skills.gist: Where the data lives, and why the choice locks you in.
need: SQL (relational): structured, good for data with clear relationships and reporting.
NoSQL: flexible shape, good for scale and simple lookups.
Changing the data model after launch is expensive. The early choice matters.
skills.assess: I can name one reason to choose a SQL database and one reason to choose NoSQL.

skills.name: Client vs server
skills.gist: What runs on the phone vs what runs on your machines.
need: Client = the app or browser. Server = the backend you control.
A server change ships instantly. A client change waits for an app-store update.
In India this matters — many users sit on old app versions for months.
skills.assess: I can explain why a bug fixed on the server reaches users faster than one fixed in the mobile app.

skills.name: Latency & caching
skills.gist: Why things feel slow, and the main trick to fix it.
need: Latency is the delay before a response. Test on a real phone on 4G, not office wifi.
Caching stores a copy of a common answer so it isn't recomputed every time.
The risk: a stale cache serves an old answer after the real data changed.
skills.assess: I can explain what caching does and name one case where a stale cache would cause a bug.

skills.name: A/B tests
skills.gist: How you prove a change caused an outcome instead of coinciding with one.
need: Split users at random, change one thing, compare the two groups.
Fix the success metric and the run length before you start, not after you peek.
"Significant" means the gap is unlikely to be noise — which needs enough users.
skills.assess: I can explain why you fix the success metric and sample size before starting an A/B test, not after.

skills.name: SQL
skills.gist: Pulling your own numbers instead of waiting on an analyst.
need: SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, JOIN covers most of what a PM needs.
Practice on a real dataset — a weekend on Mode's tutorial is enough to start.
A PM who can query is faster and much harder to mislead.
skills.assess: Given the table, I could write a query to count sign-ups per day for the last week.

skills.name: Data pipelines
skills.gist: How a number gets from a user's tap to your dashboard.
need: Events are logged, moved, processed, and loaded somewhere you can query.
Any step can fail or lag — so the number can be wrong even if users are fine.
When a metric looks off, first question: is it real, or did tracking break?
skills.assess: When a metric looks wrong, I'd check whether tracking or the pipeline broke before assuming user behaviour changed.

skills.name: ML features
skills.gist: What a PM owns when the feature is a model — recommendations, ranking, fraud.
need: A model needs training data, an objective to optimise, and a baseline to beat.
Cold start: a new user or new item has no history, so the model guesses badly.
A model can optimise the wrong thing — watch time instead of satisfaction.
skills.assess: I can explain what training data is and why a recommendation model needs an objective and a baseline.

skills.name: Non-functional requirements
skills.gist: "It works" vs "it works under load, stays up, keeps data safe."
need: The categories: performance, scalability, availability, security, reliability.
Before a big launch (a sale), set a target for each and load-test against it.
Decide what degrades gracefully — e.g. recommendations fail, checkout never does.
skills.assess: Before a high-traffic launch I could state a target for load and uptime, and say what happens when a dependency fails.

nonTechnical.intro: This is where interviews are won or lost. All of it is learnable now with one real product and a notebook.

skills.name: User research
skills.gist: Understanding the problem before you touch a solution.
need: Ask about the last time it actually happened, not what someone would hypothetically do.
Don't pitch your idea in the interview — you'll just hear agreement.
Five to ten conversations is usually enough to see a pattern.
skills.assess: I can run a 20-minute user interview without pitching my idea or asking leading questions.

skills.name: Prioritisation
skills.gist: Saying no to good ideas so the great ones get built.
need: Know two frameworks — RICE and Impact/Effort — and when each fits.
Filter by "does this fit the strategy" before you score anything.
Balance quick wins with a couple of bigger bets.
skills.assess: I can take five feature ideas and produce a defensible order, showing my reasoning.

skills.name: Metrics
skills.gist: Picking the number you'll be judged on — and not gaming it.
need: A North Star (the one number), plus guardrails that stop you cheating it.
Read a funnel and a retention cohort.
Total sign-ups is vanity. Weekly-active-and-retained is real.
skills.assess: For a product I use, I can name its likely North Star metric and two guardrails.

skills.name: Writing
skills.gist: Most PM work is writing. A clear one-pager saves weeks.
need: A spec has: the problem, who it's for, what success looks like, what's out of scope.
An engineer should be able to estimate it without a meeting.
Short sentences. No jargon.
skills.assess: I can write a one-page spec an engineer could question and estimate without a meeting.

skills.name: Stakeholder comms
skills.gist: Getting things done with no authority over anyone.
need: Update people regularly, not only when something breaks.
When a date slips, say it early with the reason and the new plan.
Leadership wants the outcome; engineers want the detail. Tailor it.
skills.assess: I can write a status update that states a slipped timeline plainly and says what I'm doing about it.

skills.name: Business sense
skills.gist: A product makes money or it dies. Think like an owner.
need: Size a market out loud, stating each assumption.
Unit economics: does one more customer make or lose money?
Tie every feature back to revenue, retention, or growth.
skills.assess: I can estimate the market size for a product out loud, stating each assumption.
